speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1960, was presented by Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to table the main estimates for the fiscal year 1959-60. Following the example set by my predecessor, Mr. Abbott, in 1950, 1951 and 1954 I propose to make a statement to the house now for the purpose of drawing to the attention of hon. members certain significant features of these estimates.
The most noteworthy feature is that compared with those for the present year, 195859, these estimates provide for a decrease of $39.1 million in the non-statutory items. This decrease reverses a trend of some years' duration. I am glad to report to the house that although this reduction was not accomplished without painstaking effort it has been achieved without any reduction in essential services to the public.
The second significant feature of these estimates is that the government has maintained the level of expenditure designed to assist national development and employment opportunities. Thus it may be seen that in its approach to the financial requirements in the fiscal year commencing April 1 next the government has endeavoured to maintain and foster a high degree of economic activity on the one hand and to exercise the restraint and balance necessary in coping with the inflationary aspects of recovery on the other hand.
Total budgetary expenses contemplated in the estimates for the new fiscal year amount to $5,595,848,557. This total, which includes both expenditures already authorized by continuing statutes and moneys parliament is being asked to appropriate, is compared in the blue book with a total of $5,295.6 million which was the sum provided for in the main, supplementary and further supplementary estimates No. 1 for the current year. Since the main estimates for 1959-60 were printed there have been tabled in the 66968-9-45
house further supplementary estimates No. 2, providing for additional expenditures in the present fiscal year of $28 million, so that the comparable total for 1958-59 now becomes $5,323.6 million, resulting in an over-all increase of $272.2 million. These figures do not include amounts for deficits in the old age security fund, since it is the practice to make such provision in the final supplementary estimates.
The government's approach to the task of preparing the 1959-60 estimates may be of interest to the house. Last year in order to provide employment the government deliberately favoured expenditure which would provide work through construction programs of a capital nature. This year we have expedited and encouraged programs which will provide work this winter. But we have been careful to ensure that we do not add to or extend a program which would build up government overhead without creating immediate employment. On all other items in the estimates our aim has been to apply a firm hand in restraining controllable expenditure without sacrificing essential public services.
There is an increase of $311.3 million in the estimates in the statutory area. It is attributable substantially to two or three items. First is the sum of $160 million for payments to the provinces under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. The second is an increase of $106 million for statutory public debt charges. This increase may be attributed in approximately equal measure to the increase in the total public debt outstanding and higher rates of interest. In the third place is an increase of $25 million for family allowances, due to the increase in the numbers of those eligible, and $9 million for unemployment assistance attributable to the expected lag in the settlement of claims relating to the current fiscal year.
The over-all decrease of $39.1 million in the non-statutory items was achieved in spite of an increase of $88 million in the cost of administration and operation of all departments. This increase of $88 million is attributable to four items: first, an increase of $20 million in civil salaries and wages; second, an increase of $22 million in the pay and allowances of the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; third, an increase of $19 million in the cost of repairs and upkeep of equipment; and

Tabling of Main Estimates fourth, smaller increases spread over a number of other items due principally to rising costs.
Notwithstanding the increases of $42 million in salaries and wages and pay and allowances, there has been no appreciable expansion in the strength of the civil service of Canada or of the defence forces. While additional responsibilities have been assumed, the overall increase in the size of the government establishment for 1959-60 will be only .4 per cent over 1958-59. This is the smallest annual growth shown since 1951. It demonstrates the government's continuing effort to increase efficiency and at the same time to economize on the use of staff.
The principal factor in the increases in expenditures for administration is the fact that, in addition to the normal effect of reclassification and annual increases, there has been a continuation of the trend toward improved recruiting into the public service and armed forces, and toward lower rates of turnover within the authorized establishment. This has been particularly noticeable in relation to technical and professional grades which are being attracted into the public service within the approved staff strength.
The third factor, namely $19 million for repairs and upkeep of equipment, reflects an intensification of government programs of maintenance and repair.
Another factor contributing to the increased cost of administration is an amount of $8.9 million for travel and removal expenses, notably in national defence. Expenditures under this head are higher in certain years to meet the requirements for larger scale movement of forces. In the forthcoming year a large part of the brigade will be replaced in Europe in the normal rotation pattern.
The capital program reveals an over-all decrease in contemplated expenditure of $65 million. However, it is anticipated that the level of capital expenditure achieved in the current year by most of the civil departments will be maintained, particularly in those areas where expenditures are related to resource development and to employment, such as the departments of agriculture, mines and technical surveys, and northern affairs and national resources. The capital provision for the Department of Public Works is reduced in consequence of the accelerated completion of many public buildings and the inevitable time lag in the completion of plans for new projects. The provision in the Department of Transport, however, will remain at the present high level which has been established to meet the urgent requirements of civil aviation. The decline in the capital program of the public works department is largely offset

by the provisions for the Department of Transport. Thus the government is maintaining a high volume of national works to continue the battle against unemployment.
The requirements of the Department of National Defence on capital account are also reduced. Expenditures in this area, apart from new requirements, are governed by the progress of various long-term defence projects.
Parliament is being asked to provide for loans, investments and advances-which add to the government's active assets-totalling $122,887,799 in addition to those for which continuing authority exists.
Not included in the figures I have thus far mentioned, but noted in the volume of estimates for consideration, are the forecast amounts for old age security pension payments totalling $577,600,000. These payments are not treated as budgetary expenditures since they are payable out of the old age security fund.
The house will see that in planning its spending program for 1959-60 the government sought, within the limits of controllable expenditure, to restrain inflation while at the same time assisting employment and the development of resources.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill):
That the message of His Excellency, together with the estimates presented this day, be referred to the committee of supply.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, not having had the advantage of an opportunity to study the minister's statement and the estimates which have just been tabled, it is impossible for me to comment at any length at this time on those estimates. But in view of what the minister has said perhaps it is appropriate for us on this side of the house to point out that the amount of the decrease in controllable expenditures, which seems to be about $32 million-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is $39.1 million.

-as the minister points out, $39.1 million, is a small amount indeed compared with the figure of $500 million which we used to hear advanced by those now on the other side of the house as to what could be done about reducing controllable expenditures without interfering with essential services. While, of course, we welcome that reduction if it does not interfere with any essential services, it is only fitting to point out that in these estimates, which I think are the highest peacetime estimates in our

history-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong-there is an increase of $272 million over last year, not taking into account the increase of $22 million in expenditures from the old age security fund.
The minister has also emphasized, Mr. Speaker, that the civil service salaries and allowances have been kept well in check. I would point out, however, that during the year there has been an increase of some 4,000 in the number of civil servants, a fact which also is interesting in the light of what hon. gentlemen opposite used to say about reducing the number of civil servants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is confused there.
Oh, no.
I suggest that these estimates which have been put before us emphasize the desirability of the budget being brought down in order to deal with them at the earliest possible moment.

Mr. Speaker, like the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) we did not have the estimates before us until just a few minutes ago. I would make the suggestion to the government that in future, when the minister makes a very long and comprehensive statement on this subject, it would be a common courtesy if we could have a confidential advance copy of the estimates, as we are given by courtesy an advance copy of the speech from the throne as delivered by His Excellency. I believe somebody said, "The same courtesy as the press". Of that I have no knowledge. But I think it is only fair that when the minister makes a very long statement-something of a preliminary statement to his budget address-the members of the opposition parties should have the opportunity of seeing the estimates in advance.
I think the Leader of the Opposition made some very important points in his short statement. I noted that the minister forecast a decrease in ordinary expenditures of just $39 million, which is a very small amount in relation to the very vigorous statements that we had over the years as to the hundreds of millions of dollars which could be saved if the government squeezed out expenditures which were wasteful and extravagant. The cold, hard fact is that the government has been able to save only a small proportion of that amount it said it would save when it was in the opposition.
We note that total expenditures are going up. Most of those increases we support. As a matter of fact we have played a very active part over the years in promoting some of the increases we have here. I refer particularly 66968-9-45J
Tabling of Main Estimates to the $160 million that will be an additional expenditure to provide hospitalization insurance in various provinces. Although this is an increase in expenditure, and although this would result, normally at any rate, in a similar increase in taxes, we in the C.C.F. feel that this increase is an excellent expenditure and a good investment by the Canadian public. We go further and say that we think the estimates now before us demonstrate once again that no matter what may be the public statements of the party in power to the effect that the government should have a small role in the economic field, the modern trend is for government expenditures to increase and for the government's role in the economy to be expanded. Even under a Conservative government we see that this is the case.
I would suggest that there are other increases and expenditures at this time that the Canadian public would support, and support cheerfully, and I would suggest for one the provision of a comprehensive national health insurance plan. I believe the Canadian nation would support such a program. We do not support the increase that has been made necessary because of increased interest charges on the government debt. We feel that this is an expenditure that was not necessary, an expenditure that should not have been incurred, and a surprising expenditure in light of the Conservative party's record over the years in advocating loose money and lower interest charges instead of the present tight money and high interest policy. We will in the days ahead study these estimates thoroughly and make our detailed contributions on their various aspects.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Minister of Finance will inform the house as to whether or not prior to the opening of the house he gave to anyone, other than the government, copies of the estimates and copies of the written statement which he proposed to read and did read to the house when it opened.

subtopic: LACHINE CANAL

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: LACHINE CANAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have received
numerous inquiries from Montreal members of parliament regarding the future operation of the Laehine canal, I should like to make a short statement about it.
Officials of my department, of the St. Lawrence seaway authority and of the national harbours board recently met with officials of the Montreal port council and informed them that it is the decision of the government that the Laehine canal shall be kept open throughout its entire length. The purpose will be to afford access to industries situated thereon; it will not be kept open for regular through traffic going to and from the great lakes.
However, should a vessel make use of the canal to serve an industry located thereon, and have some reason for leaving the canal at the opposite end from which it entered, this will be permitted under a toll structure related to the seaway toll structure for equivalent through movement.

The canal will be transferred to the St. Lawrence seaway authority for administrative and operational purposes, but not on the basis that the seaway must run it as a selfsustaining operation. My department is maintaining financial responsibility for the Lachine canal and will provide in its estimates the funds necessary for its operation. This will make it clear that the decision to keep the canal open on the basis I have indicated is a government decision rather than a matter solely within the hands of the seaway authority to determine.
I understand that the representatives of the Montreal port council expressed themselves as satisfied with this arrangement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FILING OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Broome (Vancouver South) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FILING OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-22, to amend the Companies Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FILING OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FILING OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to prevent public companies taking advantage of the exemption given in section 121 of the Companies Act to private companies-among other requirements, those not having more than 50 shareholders-by which these so-called "family" companies do not have to file annual financial statements with the Secretary of State. Under the present definitions and section 121, large companies are able to avoid filing annual financial statements by incorporating private companies and becoming shareholders therein.
The present section 121 follows that in the pre-1948 United Kingdom companies act; however, in 1948 the United Kingdom act was revised and a provision was inserted to remedy the situation in England. The Canadian act was amended in some respects to follow the 1948 English revision, but this provision was not adopted. The proposed amendment, adapted to the United Kingdom act, would insert the United Kingdom provision in section 121 of the Canadian act. The amendment would not affect the true "family" private company.
It is proposed that the amendment come into effect on January 1, 1960 to give adequate notice to interested persons.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct the attention of the house to salted codfish. Yesterday the hon. member for Gloucester asked me about a statement attributed to Hon. Wills O. Isaacs at a banquet in Jamaica. The statement Mr. Isaacs made there was:
We have come to a definite agreement and understanding so in future there will be no more cause for complaints and hardship.
He was talking about the price of Canadian salted fish in the Jamaican market. The answer to my hon. friend's question is as follows. Discussions have been carried on during recent months with the minister of trade and industry of the government of Jamaica with a view to withdrawal of the retail price ceiling imposed on the sale of salted codfish in the Jamaican market. As a result of these discussions the government of Jamaica in November last did raise the retail price ceiling on salted codfish from 1 shilling 5 pence to 1 shilling 6 pence per pound.
During the recent Canadian trade fair held at Kingston, Jamaica, my colleague the Minister of Fisheries held further discussions with the Jamaican minister of trade and industry concerning the situation created by the continuance of the retail price ceiling. The day following the announcement officials of my department present at the trade fair visited the minister of trade and industry, Mr. Isaacs, and attempted to secure a commitment date for withdrawal of retail price ceilings on salted codfish in Jamaica. It is hoped that

Inquiries of the Ministry the government of Jamaica will find it possible to do away with the price ceiling, and we will continue to press for its removal.

In view of the publicly expressed horrific concern of the senior officials of the minister's department with respect to this personal opinion, and in view of the reported full inquiry into this matter, undertaken with the consent of the minister, can the minister inform the house of all the facts surrounding this case, the result of the investigation and of any action taken because of this expression of personal opinion by a public servant;-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMENT ON STATEMENT RESPECTING U.S. SATELLITE
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. The investigation into the case of Mr. Argyle revealed that because of his technical knowledge he was often assigned the task of replying to the inquiring public and newspapermen on such matters as meteors and satellites. He was telephoned at his home on a Saturday by a local newspaperman inquiring about the reception of radio signals from the new satellite. He used the occasion to express a personal opinion, criticizing the United States publicity concerning the satellite and the President's message from it.
We believe that Mr. Argyle's action is reprehensible because of the brashness of his

statements and the offensive expressions he used and particularly because of the occasion he used of a press reporter's call to him to make such statements.
I wish to read, if I may, Mr. Speaker, the letter which was sent to this employee. It reads as follows:
Ottawa, January 5, 1959
Mr. P. E. Argyle,
Dominion Astrophysical Observatory,
Royal Oak, British Columbia.
Dear Mr. Argyle:
It is very regrettable, to say the least, that you should have chosen to express to an inquiring reporter that personal opinion on the United States Atlas satellite which has made the headlines in all the Canadian press. This has proven most embarrassing to our dominion observatories, to our minister and department, and to the government as a whole.
Any civil servant has a right to entertain personal opinions, but there is an unstated rule of prudence and reticence which applies, and which you have seriously disregarded. There is no excuse for the occasion you have chosen-a call from a press reporter-for the unfortunate statements you have made.
Were it not for your good record and reputation with our department, our minister would have wished to go further than this simple reprimand and cautioning.
I am sure you have, by now, realized-

subtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMENT ON STATEMENT RESPECTING U.S. SATELLITE
speechtext: Fascism.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMENT ON STATEMENT RESPECTING U.S. SATELLITE

-the extent of the embarrassment you have caused, and that you will be governed accordingly in the future.
Yours very truly,

Canadian Citizenship Act member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) were put there. They did have very considerable administrable convenience. In fact they worked no particular hardship upon any resident citizen of Canada. Indeed, I think they worked no hardship on anyone anywhere in the world.
During the three years I was minister of citizenship and immigration no one ever suggested to me that any such change should be made. At the time I introduced certain amendments in this house to the citizenship act, it was not suggested from any part of this house that this would be a desirable change. During the spring and summer of 1957 it did come to my notice, as I think it came to the notice of many other hon. members, that there was in certain parts of this country amongst naturalized citizens-where this idea originated I do not know-a feeling that in some way or other they did not have equal status legally, that there were circumstances in which they could lose their citizenship, circumstances which did not exist in the case of a natural bom citizen.
There was a good deal of discussion on this subject during the year 1957, and it was referred to in the house by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), on a date which I could find, but I do not think there will be any dispute about it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF NATURALIZED CITIZENS

If hon. gentlemen would like to hear the answer I have no objection to giving it. Of course I never said what the hon. gentleman said, and no newspaper ever said I did. Perhaps that largely disposes of the matter. What I did say, and what I have never apologized for saying, and what I have never found any immigrant misunderstanding, was that as a means of increasing the population of a country, other things being equal, the cradle was a better way than migration because it was easier for people born and brought up in a country to adapt themselves to that country. I have never met any immigrant who had a child in this country, and to whom I explained what I really did say, who did not thoroughly agree with that view. I fully expect that the usual distortions of my statement, which I might say gave me a certain notoriety in this country that I did not have before, will go on being repeated. Being a politician, perhaps that additional notoriety may not do me any more harm than the repetition of my name may do me good.
It does seem to me, sir, that this is a rather small kind of intervention in the consideration of a subject that ought to be considered on a high level and very dispassionate on both sides of the house. I hope this bill can be considered in this way.
When the question came to my attention in the summer of 1957 I, as a former minister -and as I am sure the hon. lady would agree-naturally consulted the department, as I am sure she would in similar circumstances, in order to see what their views were. The administrative conveniences of the law as it then stood were put forward in strong terms by the department. I am not going to go into that matter, because it is not particularly relevant and because all those considerations have been removed by the decision made by the house at the last session. But against this consideration it was easy to see that if there was on the part of citizens of Canada who had come here voluntarily to make this country their home a feeling that in any way whatsoever they were not considered to be the equals of those who were born here, and if it was possible for parliament to change that feeling, we ought to try to do it.
I consulted two distinguished former members of this house. One of them was still a member of this house at that time, and the other was a member of the other place. Both of them were immigrants. I refer to Senator Croll and Hon. James Sinclair. I consulted them about this question and said to them, "Do you as immigrants feel that you are in any way inferior, legally or in any other way?" They said, "Personally


we do not, but we see the point and we think the situation should be changed."
I must say that as far as I was concerned, the judgment of those two experienced public men influenced me strongly. I felt that any small administrative inconvenience should not be weighed in the balance against an act which would give to all our citizens a feeling that there was a genuine psychological equality as between naturalized and natural bom citizens. That view was taken when the subject came up for discussion at the convention of our party in January 1958. The relevant provision of our program is contained in one sentence which I should like to put on the record, and I do so in no partisan sense. It is as follows:
The Liberal party which sponsored the Canadian Citizenship Act stands for the absolute equality of all Canadians whether bom in Canada or naturalized.
I do not think it is a partisan question at all. I understand it is the position taken by the Conservative party. If I am wrong I should be glad to be corrected by anyone authorized to speak for the party. I believe it is the position taken by the Conservative party and I hope it is the position taken by that party. I believe it is also the position taken by the C.C.F. party. If my memory serves me-and I must confess I did not read his speech right through-I think the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) took that position on the very last day of the last session or the day next to the last day. In any case it is my belief that so far as the objective of this bill is concerned, there is unanimity among all the parties in this house and, I hope, among all the members in this house.
In view of the unanimity that I believe exists I must say that we were disappointed, and we expressed our disappointment at the bill introduced at the last session. In fact we even divided the house on the question on the last day of the last session of parliament. At that time I moved an amendment in committee, and the amendment I moved at that time was in the precise terms of the bill now before the house. In order to save the time of hon. members I should like to read what I said about that amendment, because it was put quite briefly. I said this, as found at pages 4759 and 4760 of Hansard for 1958:
The only difference between what I am suggesting and what the hon. lady is putting forward in her bill, now that she has taken out . . . section (c) ... is that it will no longer be competent to revoke the citizenship of the person who has been charged with the offence of treason, is outside the country and does not come back to be tried.

That is the only person whose citizenship can now be revoked under the law as it now stands, except a person who has obtained his citizenship by fraud. As will be seen by an examination of this bill, the question of fraud is dealt with by this bill in another fashion which I think is more consonant with the real facts of the case than is the present law. With respect to this one disability, if you like to put it in that way, I said this:
That is the sort of thing that happens once in a great while. It is perhaps desirable to be able to do this.
That is to say, to revoke the citizenship of someone who is charged with treason and who will not come back to Canada to be tried. I continued:
However-
And I think this is the really important thing.
-if we are going to take away all the other reasons, why leave this one? The main purpose of this whole exercise-
That is to say, the bill which the hon. lady was then piloting through the house.
-as I take it-and I think the house is not divided on this point any longer-
I said that then, I say it now and I believe it to be true.
-is to give complete equality, the psychological feeling of equality. If a natural born person is a traitor, we cannot divest him of his citizenship. Therefore are we really going to be losing very much if once in a generation there happens to be a naturalized person who is charged with treason and is outside of Canada and whom we cannot strip of his citizenship? It does not seem to me that the country is going to suffer very much compared with what we are trying to do in this legislation. In other words, we are trying to give to the naturalized citizens of this country a feeling that once they are naturalized they are the equal of the natural born citizens.
That is still the objective. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I indicated then, as I want to indicate again today, that I am not attached to the language of this bill at all. Hon. members will recall that I drafted the amendment rather hastily. At that time I said this:
I have tried to make this suggestion in a completely non-controversial way because I think all of us are looking to the achievement of the same objective. I may say that if the Minister of Justice finds any technical defect in the amendment, I should be happy indeed to yield to his very much superior knowledge of these matters in making any textual changes in it. But I would hope that in principle it would be acceptable to the government.
I express that same hope again today, Mr. Speaker. We have now had six months in which to reflect on this matter. If, as may well be possible, the language used in
66968-9-46J
Canadian Citizenship Act the drafting of this bill is not entirely satisfactory to the government or to the law officers of the crown, I make the suggestion that we accept the principle of the bill on second reading and send it to a committee. I may say that no one will be happier than I to accept any amendment which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the Minister of Justice or the law officers of the crown think will better accomplish the objective which I believe we all have in view, namely this objective of giving to all Canadians this sense of equality.
If I may do so, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say this in conclusion. The purpose of this bill is to achieve an objective which was stated simply and eloquently by the Leader of the Opposition whose statement will be found at page 4697 of Hansard for last year. The hon. gentleman said that we should seek to achieve a situation where
-there shall be only one class of citizens in Canada, in a country which has no room for first, second or third class Canadians.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF NATURALIZED CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), remarks which were apologetic in some respects, excusing himself as the former minister of citizenship and immigration for not having dealt with something the present minister has dealt with, due to the fact that his attention was not drawn thereto. But that is beside the point. What I wish to assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. members of this house is that I as a naturalized Canadian would be, and should be, the first to go along with and support any legislation-and I quote from the explanatory notes in Bill No. C-2-that would-
-give complete equality of status with natural born citizens to citizens other than natural born citizens by removing the remaining discrimination in the present law.
Mr. Speaker, for reasons which I shall state in the course of my address I feel that this bill fails in that respect; therefore I have no alternative but to speak against it. I will vote against it and will ask the hon. members to do likewise.
As a naturalized Canadian I probably feel more strongly about any of the discriminations which exist against the thousands who are in the same category. I feel more strongly than the natural born Canadian would because, Mr. Speaker, by accepting citizenship in this country I accepted all the duties and obligations, and there is not one iota of difference between duties and obligations that are imposed upon me as a citizen and those imposed on the person who is a natural
716	HOUSE OF
Canadian Citizenship Act born Canadian. If my duties and obligations are the same, then my status should be absolutely equal to that of my brother Canadian who happens to be born in this country.
In spite of what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has said, I want to reiterate that up to last session, in September, there was discrimination against naturalized Canadians, and I wish to assure this house that naturalized Canadians did object to these discriminatory provisions in the act. Probably they missed the hon. member while he was minister of citizenship and immigration, but I can give quotations from the ethnic press for some five years back. However, that is unnecessary in the circumstances; but to refresh the memories of members, if I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from the address of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, which quotation is to be found at page 4690 of Hansard of September 5, 1958. These provisions which were discriminatory are summarized there, and I would like to put them on record. Before I do so I want to make it plain that these were the provisions under which a naturalized Canadian could have his citizenship revoked, and they were as follows:
1, assisted an enemy of Canada in time of war; 2, obtained his citizenship by false representation or fraud; 3, has resided outside of Canada for six years and has not maintained substantial connection with Canada; 4, has resided outside of Canada for two years in a country of which he was a citizen before he became a Canadian citizen and has not maintained substantial connection with Canada; 5. while out of Canada has shown disaffection or disloyalty to Her Majesty; or 6, has been convicted by a Canadian court of an offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to Her Majesty.
It is agreed that by Bill No. C-58 introduced by the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration all or practically all of these provisions were repealed. Mr. Speaker, as the law stands today I cannot find anything in the act which makes any distinction between the status of a natural born Canadian and a naturalized Canadian while in Canada. Is that right?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF NATURALIZED CITIZENS
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF NATURALIZED CITIZENS
speechtext:
They are the Canadians about whom we should be most concerned. But, Mr. Speaker, in spite of what my hon. friend has said, it is interesting to note that during all the years he was king of the castle, or minister of citizenship and immigration, he took absolutely no steps to do away with or repeal these discriminatory provisions which remained in the act, and it is only after he has landed himself in the opposition that he suddenly realizes that
{Mr. Mandziuk.]

something is required, probably through repentance, and he is now prepared to go the whole hog, which was a phrase he used in one of his addresses.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF NATURALIZED CITIZENS
speechtext: Yes, that is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF NATURALIZED CITIZENS
speechtext:
The second point which leads one to wonder, Mr. Speaker, is why did he attempt in the last session to introduce a motion which, if it had not been ruled out of order but had been accepted by the house, would have killed Bill C-58 which removed these discriminatory provisions from the act? The reason was this, "Me too, sir", as usual.
This bill, C-2 has somewhat high-sounding language. I hope hon. members will refer to it because I am going to quote, first of all, the section that it intends to repeal, and that is the section which is at present our law, section 19(1). May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to put it on Hansard for all new or naturalized Canadians to read, so they may take note of how the present law stands:
19. (1) The governor in council may. in his discretion, order that any person other than a natural-born Canadian citizen shall cease to be a Canadian citizen if, upon a report from the minister, he is satisfied that such person,
(a)	having been charged with the offence of treason under the Criminal Code or with an offence under the Official Secrets Act, has failed or refused to return to Canada voluntarily within such time as may be prescribed in a notice sent by the minister to such person at his last known address and has not appeared at the preliminary inquiry into such offence or at the trial of such offence, or both, as the case may be;
(b)	has obtained a certificate of naturalization or of Canadian citizenship by false representation or fraud or by concealment of material circumstances.
This section deals with two types of people. It deals with those who may be charged with treason or under the Official Secrets Act; and it deals, second, with those to whom a certificate of citizenship is granted but under false pretences on the part of the applicant, the concealment of material facts or other irregularities.
Let me deal with the person charged with treason. Listening to the eloquent remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate a naturalized Canadian might be led to believe that there is still discrimination in this section. But is there? If a naturalized Canadian in Canada, charged with treason, is convicted after a proper hearing in a proper court, he does not lose his citizenship. If a naturalized Canadian outside Canadian jurisdiction, or in another country, is summoned here to answer the charge of treason or a charge under the Official Secrets Act and appears to answer to that charge, he does not lose his citizenship. But a naturalized Canadian who refuses to come back to this country-the country of his adoption, the

country which accepted him and which he accepted-and stays away, declining to face the charge, loses his citizenship.
I do not know why we should be too much concerned about giving these characters- they are few in number, I admit-the protection of our diplomatic services in other countries when they have committed a breach of trust with the country which has adopted them as her own sons.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF NATURALIZED CITIZENS
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Marquette permit a simple factual question? My question is this. Looking at the words which the hon. member read, why does he think it should be possible for the governor in council to take citizenship away from a naturalized citizen in these circumstances and not from a natural born citizen?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF NATURALIZED CITIZENS
speechtext:
I intend to make reference to that. I shall have that in mind in the course of my address. I regret that we have no such provision which would affect a natural born Canadian. I regret it, and I would be in complete accord with such a provision. Mr. Speaker, permit me to quote the wording of the oath which an applicant for Canadian citizenship takes:
I	swear that I will be faithful and bear
true allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, her heirs and successors, according to law, and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada and fulfil my duties as a Canadian citizen.
So help me God.
By refusing to answer a summons to come back to this country and face-in plain language-the music, a man shows that he has no regard for Canadian law, and that he has no regard for the sovereign to whom he swore allegiance. In other words, by the very fact that he stays out of the country he convicts himself as a traitor. Mr. Speaker, I speak for the thousands and thousands of naturalized Canadians when I say that they have no respect for traitors. In particular, those who have acquired citizenship only recently, those who have come here from behind the iron curtain, know full well that it is because of traitors and quislings that the freedom of their countries was lost. I venture to dare anyone to prove that naturalized Canadians here are in favour of what the hon. gentleman has proposed.
This is the law as it stands. I am satisfied with it, and thousands of people in the same category as myself are, I believe, also satisfied with it.
The second part of this section 19 (1) which I have just quoted deals with a person who obtains a certificate by fraud, a person who misrepresents himself, goes under a false name, and so on. Well, the section now in the
Canadian Citizenship Act act sets out that a commission should hear the case, and that if it is well founded the citizenship papers should be revoked and the person concerned considered as if he had never been a Canadian citizen.
Having paid some attention to the law as it stands, let us now look at the terms of Bill No. C-2 sponsored by the hon. gentleman. I should like to put this on record, too, in Hansard if I am permitted:
19 (1) A Canadian citizen other than a natural born citizen shall not lose his citizenship for any cause for which a natural born citizen would not lose his citizenship.
Where it is established to the satisfaction of the court that a person has obtained a certificate of naturalization or Canadian citizenship by false representation or fraud or by concealment of material circumstances such certificate shall be revoked and such person shall be deemed never to have been a Canadian citizen.
Bill C-2 has not too much quarrel with the present law in so far as it affects citizens who have obtained their naturalization certificates by fraud, misrepresentation or concealment of material facts. The hon. gentleman in this bill foresees the same ultimate result, namely that somebody or other is going to make a declaration that a person had never become a citizen, which is what we have now.
In spite of the fact that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was very apologetic about the way this bill was drawn up, I cannot help but give it the respect it deserves and use the wording it contains. Now I shall deal with the revocation of citizenship of one who has obtained his citizenship by fraud, misrepresentation and so on. The bill says:
Where it is established to the satisfaction of the court-
Those hon. gentlemen who are learned in the law know that putting the definite article "the" before the noun "court" indicates a definite court, some specific court. I should like to know what court the sponsor of this bill had in mind. In section 2(b) of the act there is a definition of the court which deals with matters under the citizenship act, and I quote from section 2(h):
"Court" means any superior, circuit, county or district court, and includes in the province of Quebec any district magistrate, and in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon Territory, any stipendiary magistrate or any other person designated by the governor in council under this act.
He receives his authority for revoking citizenship from the governor in council. The procedure is set out in section 19 (1), (a), subsections 3 and 4. One of the members of the commission must have some experience in judicial matters. There is no designation in this bill as to who shall compose the

Canadian Citizenship Act court. The present law contains the procedure which must be followed leading to revocation, but there is no procedure laid down in this bill at all. By deleting the preamble of the present law the hon. member has taken out the procedure as to who may initiate proceedings and what happens to them.

The bulk and the body of this bill make very attractive reading, Mr. Speaker. It will look well on the hustings; it will sound well in a political gathering and on the platform that the hon. gentleman sponsored a bill which says:
A Canadian citizen other than a natural-born citizen shall not lose his citizenship tor any cause for which a natural-born citizen would not lose his citizenship.

I draw the attention of the house to the fact that Bill C-2 conflicts with section 18 of the act, which the sponsor of the bill should have repealed by his amendment. May I read section 18 so that it will be on Hansard. This is in direct conflict with the bill now before us, namely Bill C-2. Section 18 reads:
Subject to subsections (2) and (3), a person who, since becoming a Canadian citizen, has resided outside of Canada for a period of 10 consecutive years ceases to be a Canadian citizen upon the expiration of such period.

The rather devastating speech of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk), to which we have just listened, should add more weight to the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, a suggestion that I also made in an earlier proceeding in the house. Many public bills sponsored by private members are not drafted in properly acceptable form and may not be in complete conformity with other sections of the act they seek to amend or with other acts but nonetheless I suggest that if bills are poorly worded that should be overlooked and an attempt made to get at their essence. I suggested on another occasion that we should not be too critical of the wording of such bills and that after they receive second reading they should be referred to a standing committee of the house which could deal with all the ramifications and interconnections between the bill under consideration and any other acts then in force. That committee would be able to consult with and draw upon the experience of departmental officials and the people who deal with the drafting of bills and we would thus be able to get correctly worded legislation which would in fact reflect the announced intention or purpose of the bill.
Canadian Citizenship Act
Whether or not the bill now before us achieves that purpose is a debatable point. In my opinion there is conflict in some degree between the amendment sought and the announced purpose of the bill. Amendments were made to the act last session but if we had not had to consider them in the last few days of a lengthy session at a time when we were sitting on Saturday and also every morning and evening probably more consideration could have been given to the thoughts I should like to express with respect to the proposal now before us and the manner in which we can amend the act to meet the announced purpose of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
I am sure that all of us agree with the purpose of bringing about equality of status between natural born and naturalized citizens. I had rather hoped that the bill might have been drafted in a little better form and that it would have covered the suggestions which I intend to make. I am sure it would then have met the desire of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and would have been acceptable to the minister and to the hon. member for Marquette.
Before I go into that matter, I should like to point out that the hon. member for Marquette, speaking, as I said, in a very devastating way, made a complete analysis of the effect the amendment would have in the light of other sections of the act as it now stands. Apart from his introductory remarks and his personal interest in the subject as a naturalized Canadian citizen, he based his entire objection to the bill on the matter of a naturalized citizen refusing to return to Canada after having been charged with an offence. He did refer to section 18 but if there is any discriminatory feature involved that could easily be straightened out by a standing committee of the house in line with the purpose and intention behind the bill.
The act makes little reference, I submit, to refusing to return even though it can be inferred. Too much emphasis was placed by the hon. member on the matter of refusal to return to justify a position contrary to the idea expressed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
If I may do so, Mr. Speaker, and I think I will be within the rules as others have already done so-I am sure you will correct me if I am wrong-I should like to refer to section 19 (1) (a) of the act which says that a person shall cease to be a Canadian citizen if he has done certain things. He shall cease to be a Canadian citizen if he "having been charged with the offence of treason under the criminal code or with an offence under the Official Secrets Act, has failed or refused

Canadian Citizenship Act to return to Canada voluntarily within such time as may be prescribed in a notice sent by the minister."
I think we should examine the question of failure to return. So far as the section of the act which the bill intends to amend is concerned, during the last session I had quite a lengthy discussion with officers and members of the Canadian citizenship council, not only about the effect of this proposal but the effect of another amendment proposed last session which the minister was kind enough to withdraw. We should apply ourselves to drafting legislation in compliance with the announced intention of the bill which I am sure coincides with the intention of every member of the house, namely to give complete equality of status to natural born and naturalized citizens. I do not think there is any difference between us so far as that being our hope but if we are to draft a law that will fulfil that intention I submit we should approach the present section of the act not from the point of view expressed in this bill by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate but with this thought in mind.
Let us take the example of a naturalized Canadian citizen who may hold a very responsible position in a corporation, a profession or even in the civil service. Let us say that he departs from Canada for business, professional or other reasons and shortly after his departure a charge is laid against him for treason or an offence under the Official Secrets Act about which he had no knowledge at the time of his departure. Let us say that the charge is laid only a day or two after he leaves. He may be in the position of having made arrangements to be away from the country for business or professional reasons for a lengthy period of time. Now, I know that the minister who now heads this department would be very generous in circumstances of that nature and would give a very lenient interpretation to the section I have just described. However, we may not have this hon. lady as minister of this department forever. The mortality rate in politics is very high. If she does not fall by the wayside at election time, she may be elevated to a higher post, or indeed this government may not be the government at that time.
We should draft our legislation in this connection with these circumstances in mind. Provision should be made for the extension of the time period during which a person may be away from the country, depending on certain circumstances, and it should not be left to the generosity or lack of it of the particular minister who may be in office at that time. If we were to legislate that a person may return to Canada within a certain


period of time, if there is a preliminary inquiry into such offence or a trial, the period of time could be based on the normal length of time it takes between the laying of the charge and the case coming to court, and could take into account also travelling conditions between this country and other countries. In addition, arrangements could be made so that the governor in council may extend that period if the person makes application to have it extended. I believe this would completely meet the announced purpose of this particular bill.

If a Canadian citizen is abroad and refuses to return, I submit that any time he sets foot within the British commonwealth of nations or certain other countries extradition proceedings can be taken to bring him back to Canada to stand trial. By revoking the citizenship of a naturalized Canadian under the same circumstances I submit that you make it practically impossible for him to return and be tried and hence you make it practically impossible for this country to punish him. Looking at the situation in that light, it could be argued that you were in fact giving the advantage to the naturalized Canadian.
However, such an argument may be called farfetched. Indeed, a great many of the arguments which are advanced on this bill may be called farfetched, whether they be for or against, because how often in the past or how often in the future will the situation arise where this section in fact will have to be invoked? I think that should be taken into consideration.
Of course, the hon. gentlemen to my right may say that because of that fact the section will not be used very often, or may not be used at all, so why have it on the statute books? Of course, one could get into an endless series of arguments along that line. Why, for instance, have certain sections in the Criminal Code under which we do not prosecute very often? I submit that this section should be on the statute books in case the situation does arise, and then extraordinary action will not have to be taken at that time.
I suggest that naturalized Canadians coming to this country will back this section, because they know what it is like to have traitors among them. They know, as we all do, who our potential enemy is, namely the people who believe in the communist ideology. Naturalized Canadians who have seen this ideology and have seen the actions of men who believe in it would certainly not tolerate any person who follows that ideology and becomes a traitor to this country.
I submit that this bill is an attempt by the Liberal party once again to charge our government and our party with being discriminatory to certain groups or individuals in this country. When the people of this country are told, and when it is emphasized to them, that the only time a naturalized citizen's certificate of citizenship may be revoked is when he is charged with treason and refuses to return to stand trial; when that is communicated to all of the naturalized citizens in this country they will back the legislation 100 per cent.

I also submit, Mr. Speaker, although I may be anticipating, that if the Liberal party or any of its members label this section in our act discriminatory to naturalized Canadians residing in Canada they are doing a disservice to this country which is comparable to the disservice they are doing by their cries about unemployment and other matters affecting our economy.
Therefore, I find that for two reasons I cannot support this bill. Firstly, because it would place confusion into the Canadian Citizenship Act, and I suggest that, no matter how much amending was done, I doubt if it would accomplish the purpose that the proposer intends. Secondly, I feel that the naturalized Canadians in Canada will not tolerate, any more than any of the rest of us, a person who commits treason and then refuses to stand trial.

This bill, in effect, contains the proper safeguards which will ensure to all Canadians, whatever their origin, complete equality in letter as well as in spirit. Mr. Speaker, when one first looks at this bill he would probably believe it to be a worthwhile bill to present to the house. The only impression one would draw from reading the bill is that there is at present discrimination in Canada between natural born and naturalized Canadians.
Then if we read in the explanatory notes the purpose of the measure, we would probably think that it is a great deal more commendable, for the purpose as set out is to give complete equality of status with natural born citizens to citizens who are other than natural born by removing discriminations which now exist in the law.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mand-ziuk) has pointed out that if this bill were accepted there would in consequence arise direct conflict with section 18 of the present act which provides quite another ground upon which the citizenship of a naturalized Canadian may be taken away-not by revocation, but by time lapse. This will be one ground, in particular, with which this bill does not deal. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) may

Canadian Citizenship Act at this very moment be considering the introduction of an amendment to repeal section 18 of the act in order to make this bill more acceptable to the house. However, I would point out that section 18 and section 19 (1) are only some of the grounds upon which a naturalized Canadian could lose his citizenship. In addition there are also grounds upon which a natural born Canadian may lose his citizenship and I would refer in particular to section 4 of the act, which reads as follows:
4. A person born before the 1st day of January, 1947, is a natural born Canadian citizen
(a)	if he was born in Canada or on a Canadian ship and had not become an alien before the 1st day of January, 1947; or
(b)	if he was born outside of Canada elsewhere than on a Canadian ship and his father, or in the case of a person born out of wedlock, his mother
(1)	was born in Canada or on a Canadian ship and had not become an alien at the time of that person's birth, or
(ii) was, at the time of that person's birth, a British subject who had Canadian domicile, if, before the 1st day of January 1947, that person had not become an alien, and has either been lawfully admitted to Canada for permanent residence or is a minor.
Section 6 goes on-and remember this applies to a Canadian citizen:
6. (1) A person who is a Canadian citizen under paragraph (b) of section 4 or under paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of section 5 ceases to be a Canadian citizen upon the expiration of one year after he attains the age of twenty-one years unless, after attaining that age and before the expiration of the said year,
(a)	he asserts his Canadian citizenship by a declaration of retention thereof, registered in accordance with the regulations; and
(b)	being a national or citizen of a country other than Canada, he files in accordance with the regulations a declaration renouncing the nationality or citizenship of that country.
This is one ground which is singularly applicable to the natural born Canadian, and in consequence of which he can lose his citizenship. Moreover, it is a matter not taken into consideration in the present bill.
There is also a further ground upon which a natural born Canadian can lose his citizenship, and one which has no application whatsoever to the naturalized Canadian. I refer the house to section 20 of the present act, subsection 1:
20. (1) Where the responsible parent of a minor child ceases to be a Canadian citizen under section 15, 16, or 17, the child thereupon ceases to be a Canadian citizen if he is or thereupon becomes, under the law of any country other than Canada, a national or citizen of that country.
(2)	Where the responsible parent of a minor child ceases to be a Canadian citizen under section 18 or 19, the governor in council may, in his discretion, direct that the said child shall cease to be a Canadian citizen if he is or thereupon becomes, under the law of any country other than Canada, a national or citizen of that country.


I submit to the house that there are sections which apply exclusively to naturalized Canadians with regard to the revocation of citizenship or the losing of citizenship through time lapse. I also point out that there are sections which apply only to a natural born Canadian with regard to revocation of citizenship, or time lapse, and on this basis alone it is my contention that the bill presented to the house by the hon. member is no good at all.
The purpose of the measure is to introduce complete equality of status, and that is commendable, but how is this to be done until sections 4, 18, 20 and 19(1) of the act are repealed?
This is the first reason why I consider the bill to be a bad one, and why I cannot support it even though the principle set out is commendable. If hon. members will read through the citizenship act, as I did after this bill came to my attention-as a matter of fact I read it very thoroughly-I think they will agree with me that in Canada today, in general there is equality as between the natural born citizen and the naturalized Canadian. There are, perhaps, some occasions on which a natural born Canadian can lose his citizenship and some occasions on which a naturalized Canadian can lose his citizenship. There is not exact equality, but in general there is equality. This bill purports to do something which has already been done. I do not doubt the sincerity of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in presenting this bill to the house. I do not doubt his motives at all, but I say that in Canada today bona fide loyal Canadians, whether natural bom or naturalized who have committed no offence against the crown or against the Official Secrets Act, and who have not committed fraud in an application for citizenship, enjoy complete equality in this country.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like to say at the outset that it is not my intention to go into the legal aspects of the bill and the amendment contained therein. That has been done by my colleagues. Rather, I should like to express my opinions, impressions and observations as a naturalized Canadian. Before one can be a naturalized Canadian he must first be an immigrant. Consequently, he must meet the many requirements of the department of immigration. He must comply with the laws and other requirements of the country and he must be able to speak one of the official languages. In other words, he must have the right qualifications to be able to obtain Canadian citizenship. The citizenship that he receives entitles him to all the rights and privileges of our Canadian democratic system but he must qualify for the honour of citizenship and rightly so.
The decision of the immigrant who comes to the country was very likely precipitated by one of the following reasons. First, the economic conditions of his homeland were such that he was unable to make his living. Second, the political atmosphere and the conduct of state affairs in his homeland were such that it was unbearable for him to live under those conditions.
New immigrants who seek entry to Canada can be divided into two distinctly different groups. We find those who have a burning desire to come to Canada and make Canada their home. After they establish themselves they adapt readily to local conditions and it seems that they prosper quite well too. They seldom if ever become charges of the government. They are true immigrants and inevitably become true Canadians too.
In the other group we find people whose intentions are altogether different from those of the first group. They come here more or less for materialistic reasons. If the climate is right and they prosper reasonably soon they may stay here for a long time. They may locate in other places or eventually they may take out their citizenship papers.
Whether an immigrant comes to Canada for one reason or the other or belongs to one group or the other, his national ties with his homeland and his ties with his own people will stay with him for a long time and may never be severed entirely. This is a very dangerous situation indeed, and if he finds himself in such an unhappy position, feelings for his homeland and for his people may readily lead him to commit acts that will be detrimental to his adopted country, Canada, and eventually may result in deportation and
Canadian Citizenship Act loss of citizenship. In times of wars, revolutions or uprisings this is not uncommon. It is indeed a tragedy if he should lose his citizenship and the government should be forced to apply the laws and regulations of the Canadian Citizenship Act.
On the other hand, could one expect our government not to take the necessary steps to protect the interests of Canada and its people? The rights and privileges that the Canadian people possess did not just happen. They were achieved by these people through hard work, through sacrifices, and in many cases at the cost of their lives. Is it then unreasonable to apply to offenders the laws that are spelled out in the act which the bill before us seeks to amend?
Much as I respect the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), I cannot see any reason to amend the act by deleting paragraph (a) of subsection 1 of section 19 which now reads as follows:
(a) having been charged with the offence of treason under the Criminal Code or with an offence under the Official Secrets Act, has failed or refused to return to Canada voluntarily within such time as may be prescribed in a notice sent by the minister to such person at his last known address and has not appeared at the preliminary inquiry into such offence or at the trial of such offence, or both, as the case may be.
The listing of these offences is very important to the new Canadian, many of whom are not too familiar with the official languages and such people could interpret the provision wrongly if the section were to be amended as suggested. By having the offences listed in the act there is less chance of offences being committed. The proposed amendment reads as follows:
A Canadian citizen other than a natural born citizen shall not lose his citizenship for any cause for which a natural born citizen would not lose his citizenship. Where it is established to the satisfaction of the court that a person has obtained a certificate of naturalization or Canadian citizenship by false representation or fraud or by concealment of material circumstances such certificate shall be revoked and such person shall be deemed never to have been a Canadian citizen.
The other point that has been brought forward in argument on other occasions is that a natural born citizen is treated differently from a naturalized one. It is interpreted from this that we have first class and second class citizens in our country. In my opinion, this is indeed a very flimsy argument and one must be careful not to use it because the expression "second class citizen" could be offensive to the naturalized citizen and unjust as well. I have never heard so much about first and second class citizens as I have since coming to this chamber. I am making this assertion with some feeling. This subject has been played up so much during the last

Canadian Citizenship Act session that people who never heard of it before are beginning to wonder if there is such a thing as a first and second grade of Canadians in the opinion of some people in Canada.
Let us remember that one-third of all our population consists of stock other than English and French. About one-third of these people, at one time or another, came here as immigrants and became naturalized Canadians. They are not second class citizens. Surely, the 20,000 voters in my constituency of Humboldt-Melfort, who are of many nationalities and who voted for me, were fully aware of the fact that I am a naturalized Canadian. I must say, in all fairness and with respect for those people in my riding who voted for the other candidates, that they did so not because they did not want to be represented in parliament by a naturalized Canadian or second class citizen.
I believe every naturalized Canadian realizes that he is an adopted child of this country and is most anxious to prove himself to be a worthy member of this Canadian family. He knows that he may share not only in the benefits but must do his part to make Canada a country in which justice prevails for all citizens on an equitable basis. What I have just stated, Mr. Speaker, is not merely my own opinion about a naturalized Canadian. I should like to quote from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of January 28, in which Mrs. Laura Schippers, a Dutch born immigrant, had this to say:
Laura Schippers was so pleased at being made a citizen of Canada that she wanted to shout about it.
So, the Dutch-born Mrs. Schippers did the next best thing-she wrote about it.
She told friends here of a card she had printed and mailed to about 50 friends and kinfolk.
The inscription:
"With gratitude to God and good friends and with deep love for Canada, I hereby announce that today, after overcoming many difficulties, I had the great privilege to pledge my allegiance and loyalty to Canada and her sovereign and that from this day on I am a Canadian citizen."
Mrs. Schippers, the editor of a Dutch-language weekly newspaper published here, paid $15 to have the cards printed.
"It was my own idea," she said. "I was proud of becoming a Canadian and I wanted to tell people about it."
I am sure Mrs. Schippers could never have written the inscription on the card or spoken those words had she felt that she had not been given complete equality of status with natural born citizens. She felt that the citizenship that she received gave her the same equality as any other citizen in the country. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I must disagree with the proposed amendment to this section, and I will vote against it.

Canadian Citizenship Act of initiative to start a new life, and frequently it takes boundless energy to establish oneself in a new country. They know the story of Poland, Czechoslovakia and the three small Baltic states which disappeared so long ago, namely Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia. In other instances it is life imprisonment; and for what might be considered lesser forms of treason it is imprisonment up to a maximum of 14 years. Treason is not a light offence. In the first place fraud, which is still covered in our act, is also a reason for losing naturalization in the United Kingdom. It is covered by the British nationality act of

1948 which has provisions identical with those o f the Canadian act prior to 1958. In Australia both citizens of registration as well as citizens by naturalization can lose their citizenship if they obtain entry into the country by fraud, misrepresentation, et cetera, as we have provided in our act. The same law prevails in New Zealand. In that country the law was originated in 1928, much prior to the introduction of the law in the United Kingdom and the other more famous commonwealth countries. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the provision with regard to fraud, which is now uniform throughout the commonwealth should certainly remain in the legislation. For that reason alone I take issue with Bill No. C-2 in its present form.
While speaking on fraud, I should like to suggest that perhaps part III-that is the part which deals with loss of citizenship- could be improved upon in so far as it deals with loss of citizenship by an alleged fraud. It seems only proper for us to assume that a great many of our new Canadians who came in here after the 1945 conflict, in order to get here must have on occasion made a certain amount of so-called innocent misrepresentations. I would suggest to the government that in a subsequent amendment to part III we should, after a period of time and proof of good citizenship, condone misrepresentation of allegations which had been made, particularly so if the citizen gaining entry was from a country which had been at war with us or was coming from the Orient where the standard of entry is so rigid. Many citizens of the Orient who are relatives of Canadians are perhaps inclined to be a little bit careless in their statements in order to gain entry. I suggest to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) that some serious thought should be given to an amendment which would condone fraud after the lapse of a period of 10 or 12 years of continued good citizenship in Canada.
Dealing with the other matter, namely loss of citizenship for reasons other than fraud, I think we should consider what has taken place in these commonwealth countries which I mentioned a few minutes ago. In New Zealand there are still three reasons other than fraud by which a naturalized citizen of that country can lose his citizenship. The third one is a minor one, consisting of being convicted of an offense for which the sentence is a term of imprisonment of more than 12 months in another country after citizenship had been taken out. In Australia there 66968-9-47
Canadian Citizenship Act are still five reasons other than fraud whereby citizens of that country other than natural born citizens may lose their right to citizenship.
At the present time Canada has the fairest regulations and law with regard to loss of citizenship for reasons other than fraud. In the United Kingdom, the law is half-way between the new law of Canada of 1958 and the law of the other commonwealth countries.
In England there has been a tendency to be a little bit more relaxed because of the fact that the great percentage of the people in the old country are natural born citizens.
In the United States as in Canada our rapid growth has been not because of natural birth in this country but because of the fact that our doors have been open to the people of the world who otherwise qualify, and they have come here in great numbers.
Much has been said today about traitors. That is a subject in which all of us must at all times take a great interest. Fortunately for us in Canada today, treason is not a common crime or in any case one does not hear about it, and few charges are laid. For the benefit of the record, though, may I say that treason is still a reason for a naturalized Canadian losing his citizenship only if that person refuses to come back to Canada and face a jury of his fellow citizens.
I think that treason is the worst of all crimes. Section 46 of the Criminal Code contains six or seven paragraphs defining offences of treason. However, they can be briefly summarized as follows: attempts on Her Majesty's life; killing Her Majesty; using force or violence in Canada or in a province of Canada for the purpose of overthrowing the federal government or one of our provincial governments, et cetera. Another section follows, namely section 48 of the Criminal Code, which deals with offences of treason with regard to violence for the purpose of the overthrow of the government. This has a three-year limitation having regard to the laying of the information. At the present time, under that act it is possible for a citizen, whether natural born or naturalized or for a person who is not a citizen to escape our law unless he is brought before the court within a period of three years. What I can see happening is this. A naturalized citizen, one who came in here perhaps with the intention of being a spy, one who might be on the payroll of our future enemy, could get citizenship in Canada, commit an act of violence with a view to overthrowing this present government-which I think is the purpose of this legislation-and simply return to the country of his origin; and if a charge is not laid within three years he could escape the

Canadian Citizenship Act verdict of his jurymen. That alone is sufficient reason for keeping the offence of treason on the statute books, even if it is nothing more than an axe over the head of a very, very minor fraction of 1 per cent of the naturalized citizens of this country.
I do not intend to repeat what has been said by many members with regard to the fact that natural born citizens are getting preference over our fellow Canadians who are now naturalized citizens. I think probably it is unfair that such should be the case. I would be very much in favour of making them equal provided they attend trial. It is much easier for a naturalized citizen to become an absconding citizen and to disappear, perhaps behind the iron curtain. A Canadian of natural birth would have a limited opportunity to avail himself of that practice.
I am not opposed to seeing the law being made uniform by necessary amendments to the Criminal Code which would take away the right of citizenship from any Canadian citizen who is found guilty of such a serious crime. I think probably that would be a worthy amendment to the Criminal Code; but I do not think that legislation of that type should creep into an act which is respected and is read from time to time by our new citizens as they enter the country. I think that the Canadian Citizenship Act should be as concise as possible; that it must be understandable to people who are not necessarily entirely familiar with English or French; and that the least amount of amendment made to that legislation will mean that we, as Canadians, will be benefited. The amendment which was passed known as Bill No. C-58 of 1958 went a long way, Mr. Speaker. It was something which in all probability the mover of Bill No. C-2 should have brought in during the last four years or more when he was minister. I congratulate the government of this day in taking the step which it took in such a short period of time after its election in March of 1958.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want again to congratulate the member for Marquette and all those other members of all political faiths who have stood up here today and expressed their own beliefs without any fear of political criticism.
