I am happy to see that he is at last making the record clear and that this attempt on his part to pull the wool over the eyes of the people is beginning to fail.
We have had excellent speeches in the house this afternoon, especially from members of the legal fraternity, who have made it quite clear that our present act contains several sections which are out of keeping with the spirit-and I use the word "spirit"-which I believe most hon. members feel relative to the way in which we appreciate and are attempting to bring our naturalized Canadians to an equal status with that of other citizens in this country. I thought that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. MacLean) did a remarkable job when he pointed out that sections 4, 18, 19 and 20 were sections which might well be looked into and considered in the light of the principle which I think is universally accepted in this house.
As I see it right now, and from following very closely all afternoon the discussion which has taken place, the bill of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is one of confusion and contradiction, something for which my hon. friend, of course, has become quite notorious in recent times. The generalizations in his bill, I would say, take away more rights than they confer with respect to people for whom he now expresses such great concern.
During the last session the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) spoke in the debate on this question and he said that he would like to see one class of Canadian citizenship. I hope that he can convince the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate of this great conception with which most hon. members agree.
There was also another remarkable speaker from the opposition benches, namely the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). He had some very interesting remarks to make on the matter before the house today. He said such things as this, "Let us be stripped of die-hard political allegiance", whatever that means. I did not hear any further explanation of that sentence. Then he went on to say that he has no quarrel with the minister and is prepared to admit that the present government has been most considerate and most helpful in
Canadian Citizenship Act matters of citizenship. I am certainly happy to hear members of the Liberal party speaking that way. Then he went on to say, "We are most grateful for the amendment brought in at the last session", and yet he was one of those who voted against the amendment. He talks of stripping ourselves of die-hard political allegiance then he goes on to say something about giving the government full marks and full credit for the amendment brought in at the last session. As I said a moment ago, he voted against the amendment.
We have an idea of what we are up against in this debate on this bill. The hon. member for Cartier says on the one hand that a naturalized Canadian should not lose his citizenship, even if he leaves the country and fails to come back, if he is charged before the courts with a treasonable offence, and on the other hand he says that this house should devise some means of stripping a natural born Canadian of his citizenship. To me, that seems paradoxical because no matter how far we go in our thinking about the problem there will always be another problem.
In that regard I might point out that there are many cases where people from countries in Europe who have obtained Canadian citizenship in effect maintain a dual citizenship. Suppose we did strip a man of his citizenship for failing to comply with section 19 (1); he could still have a citizenship, the citizenship of the land in which he was born. A natural born Canadian would not have that privilege if we were to accept the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cartier. I think this is ridiculous.
No matter how far we go with the question there are certain aspects on both sides which cannot be taken, shall we say, to an arithmetical conclusion. Some common sense will always have to be applied. As I said before, the important thing is that we should display the spirit with which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration presented her amendment to the house last year, the spirit with which we have treated our naturalized citizens in the past two parliaments during which I have had the privilege of being a member of the house. It is the spirit that counts because no matter how hard we try to bring in legislation that will cover every nook and cranny no legislation is letter perfect.
I think the legislation we have now is satisfactory and I for one, coming from metropolitan Toronto an area which has many naturalized Canadians, probably a greater number than any other part of the country, have heard nothing in recent months critical in any way of the amendment the government brought in last session. As I said before,

Canadian Citizenship Act I think the hon. member tor Bonavista-Twil-lingate is trying to bring in some kind of a bogey. In fact, I think someone described it earlier as a red herring. All I can say is that I have had many opportunities to meet the people in my area and I have heard nothing of this terrible discrimination against someone who may be disloyal and who refuses to come back to Canada and clear himself of any charges which may be laid against him.
This act was introduced by the Liberal party and I was very happy to hear that it was the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who introduced the legislation in the first place. We must also be cognizant of the fact that for the last three years of the late but not lamented Liberal administration the act was administered by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, but I think we have eliminated the inequalities in the act-I think we all agree there were inequalities-in so far as it is practical to do so at the present time. I know that many naturalized Canadians express deep concern that the odd individual is able to get into the country by virtue of faulty screening, but with the human factor involved undoubtedly this will occur from time to time, and I am sure that no reasonable individual would want us at this time in our history, when we are faced with the great menace of communism, to do away with any controls in any way affecting the security of the Canadian people and our country.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to take a fresh look at the act. After all, we only amended one section at the last session of parliament. It was the worst section, but I would say that the debate today has been most useful in that other sections have been brought to light which could probably stand some review. We see cases reported in our daily newspapers about the odd person being denied the opportunity of Canadian citizenship and, according to precedent, reasons are not given. I think this is another reason why on the one hand we should try to be as tolerant as possible in giving people the opportunity to obtain Canadian citizenship while on the other hand we must maintain some kind of control to protect our security and be sure that what we do is in the best interests of the whole country.
As I said before, the act as it now stands on the statute books is probably much more generous than the faulty amendment presented today in the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In the last 10 or 12 years we have seen over a million newcomers arrive in Canada, and from my experience I want to say that most of them are

turning out to be first-class citizens and equal to those of us who are natural born. On the other hand, undoubtedly there may be the odd one in days to come who may turn out to be one of those to whom reference has been made by previous speakers. For that reason I feel that the act as it stands today, containing section 19 (1), should be left as it is rather than taking the action suggested by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on the basis of the attitude, well, what is wrong if one bad individual should get by?
I think this also involves a matter of principle. We are trying to build a great country. We have fine people who have come here to join those of us who were natural born in building the country and I think it is in the interests not only of naturalized Canadians but of natural born Canadians that we protect and maintain the high standard of Canadian citizenship. As I read the bill, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is merely splitting hairs on a very fine, minute point involving whether we should or should not forget about a certain type of individual who as a result of his actions has been charged with a certain offence and who, if he fails to respond and defend himself as any loyal Canadian should be prepared to do, may be in danger of losing his citizenship.
The true spirit of Canadian citizenship is now manifested in our act, and I have already discussed at some length the fact that there will always be little things which will neither fit this way nor that way in our laws. The best example of that was my reference to dual citizenship. Natural born Canadians do not have the opportunity to obtain dual citizenship while some naturalized Canadians do. No amount of legislation will ever change that fact because there is no way in which a natural born Canadian can obtain dual citizenship. So I say we must work toward the goal about which the Prime Minister has preached for so many years throughout the land, namely equality of opportunity for all our citizens irrespective of whether they are natural born or whether they have come here from other countries to make a home for themselves and their children. I should like to point out the paradox in the thinking of my hon. friend opposite when he says he is in favour of a cradle immigration policy. I say this thinking contravenes the laws of biology such as Mendel's law. When you have natural born Canadian citizens here, like some hon. members present, whose parents came here from other countries, then by my hon. friend's designation the ones who were born here would be first-class Canadian citizens but these children would be sons or daughters of second-class Canadian citizens.

This is not in agreement with the laws of biology.
I would conclude my remarks today by saying that the actions of this government, during the year and a half in which they have been in office, have proven beyond the shadow of a doubt where they stand on this great question of a realistic appreciation of the problems which face our naturalized Canadians. We have faced up to these problems. As I mentioned before, we did the right thing in so far as reducing the discriminatory 20-year requirement for the old age pension was concerned. These people are appreciative of that and aware of that. We did the right thing when we amended this act in 1958 by eliminating the gross errors which were put into it by my hon. friend and his colleagues of the previous Liberal administration. I want to assure my hon. friends in this house that this government, under the able leadership of one of Canada's greatest prime ministers, John Diefenbaker, will do everything possible to make sure that our naturalized Canadian citizens will enjoy equality of opportunity and equality of citizenship that natural born Canadians enjoy.

Because an order in council instituted by the hon. gentleman's own government on November 26, 1942 says this:
Any person who is a British subject by reason of marriage, or by reason of birth or naturalization in Canada, or by reason of the birth or naturalization of his father in Canada, and who makes application for repatriation to any country which at the time of application is at war with Canada, shall, as from the date of his departure from Canada for repatriation, cease to be a British subject.
Not only that individual but all the members of his family would immediately cease to be Canadian citizens even if they had been born in Canada.
